title: London Police Detain 139 Amid Massive Protests Over Palestine Action Ban, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
Police in London detained more than 130 demonstrators on Saturday after a crowd gathered to protest the government’s decision to ban the activist group Palestine Action, a move that has ignited a fresh wave of dissent across the United Kingdom. The arrests, which bring the total to at least 139 people, occurred after officers issued a clear warning that the rally would be deemed unlawful. Similar protests erupted in Edinburgh, where dozens of participants faced police scrutiny, underscoring the growing tension surrounding the controversial proscription of the organization ahead of a Supreme Court appeal.

Palestine Action, which the Home Office classified as a terrorist‑linked group in early 2024, has been at the centre of a heated debate over the limits of political protest and the definition of terrorism. The group, which describes itself as a “non‑violent solidarity movement” supporting Palestinian rights, was proscribed after a series of high‑profile actions that included blocking ports and disrupting supply chains to draw attention to the Gaza conflict. Critics argue that the ban infringes on civil liberties and criminalises legitimate dissent, while supporters of the proscription contend that the group’s tactics cross the line into illegal interference with commerce and public safety.

The London demonstration, organized by a coalition of human‑rights organisations and student groups, was intended to coincide with the scheduled hearing of a legal challenge to the ban at the UK Supreme Court. Protesters gathered outside the Metropolitan Police’s headquarters, chanting slogans and brandishing placards that read “Free Palestine Action” and “Right to protest, not to proscribe.” Police officers, equipped with riot gear, warned the crowd that the assembly violated the Terrorism Act’s restrictions on gatherings supporting proscribed entities. When the warning was ignored, officers moved in, using batons and handcuffs to detain participants. Many of those arrested were later released on bail, but the sheer number of detentions has sparked accusations of heavy‑handed policing.

Legal experts note that the Supreme Court case—brought forward by a coalition of civil‑society groups—could set a precedent for how the UK balances national security concerns with freedom of expression. Professor Amelia Hart of the London School of Economics, who specialises in counter‑terrorism law, explained that “the court will have to consider whether the Home Office’s designation of Palestine Action meets the statutory threshold for terrorism, or whether it is an overreach that stifles legitimate political activism.” The outcome may influence future proscription decisions, potentially reshaping the legal landscape for protest movements that adopt disruptive tactics.

The unrest has also reverberated beyond the capital. In Edinburgh, a smaller rally outside the Scottish Parliament saw police intervene after a similar warning was issued. While fewer arrests were reported, the incident highlighted the coordinated nature of the opposition and the willingness of activists to challenge the ban in multiple jurisdictions. Human‑rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Liberty, have condemned the arrests as a “disproportionate response” and called for an independent inquiry into police conduct.

As the Supreme Court prepares to hear arguments later this month, the government faces mounting pressure to justify its stance. Prime Ministerial spokespersons have maintained that the proscription is a necessary tool to protect national security and to deter actions that threaten critical infrastructure. Yet, public opinion appears divided, with recent polls indicating that a majority of Britons support the right to protest, even when the cause is contentious.

The coming weeks will likely determine whether the ban on Palestine Action endures or is overturned, and how far law‑enforcement agencies are prepared to go in enforcing such designations. If the court rules against the proscription, it could embolden other activist groups to adopt similar direct‑action tactics, prompting a reassessment of the legal thresholds for terrorism. Conversely, an affirmation of the ban would reinforce the state’s authority to curtail organisations deemed a security threat, potentially curbing a wave of disruptive protests. The resolution of this case will not only shape the future of Palestine Action but also signal how the UK reconciles civil liberties with security imperatives in an increasingly polarized political climate.
